wine.name: Montes Alpha M
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, about four fifths, with Cabernet Franc and smaller shares of Merlot and Petit Verdot.
wine.sites: The house's Finca de Apalta, on the granite hillsides of the Apalta horseshoe near Santa Cruz; by the house's sheets the fruit comes from the estate's steepest slopes, cropped at low yields.
wine.making: Picked into small boxes in the cool of the day and sorted by bunch and by berry, the fruit falls uncrushed by gravity into stainless steel, soaks cold for about five days and ferments for about ten. The wine then spends eighteen months in French oak barriques, all of them new in the early vintages and most of them in later ones.
wine.glass: Ripe cherry, plum and cassis with a faint note of mint, over cedar, vanilla, tobacco and toast from the oak; concentrated, with dense, silky tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable a few years after release, it can develop for twenty years and more, by the house's own sheets.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant for at least an hour, as the house advises; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Montes Alpha M is the Apalta red of Viña Montes: a Bordeaux blend led by Cabernet Sauvignon from granite hillsides near Santa Cruz, aged eighteen months in French oak. Full and silky, with cassis, cedar and a hint of mint, it rewards an hour in a decanter.
records.story: Montes began with a harvest. In 1987, by the house's own timeline, its founding winemaker and a partner picked the grapes of the first Montes Alpha Cabernet Sauvignon, and in 1988 four partners founded the company under the name Discover Wines; it soon traded as Viña Montes, after the winemaker. The partners looked for hillside ground in Colchagua, and the timeline records the purchase of their Apalta estate in 1995: a horseshoe of granite slopes near Santa Cruz, where the vines were cropped low. Alpha M followed with the 1996 vintage, a Bordeaux blend led by Cabernet Sauvignon from the estate's steepest slopes and aged in new French barriques, which the house's timeline calls Chile's first icon wine. The same hill went on to give the house's Syrah, Montes Folly, and part of its Carmenère, Purple Angel. In December 2004 Montes opened a new winery on the estate, its design based, by the house's account, on the principles of feng shui, and the fruit falls by gravity from sorting table to tank. Apalta became an area of Chile's origin decree in 2018. For a sommelier, Alpha M marks the moment a Chilean house set out to make a Cabernet blend for the cellar from one hillside.

wine.name: Clos Apalta
wine.grapes: Carmenère, from about half to two thirds, with Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, and in some years a little Cabernet Franc or Petit Verdot.
wine.sites: Old vines on the estate's Apalta hillside, planted in the early twentieth century from a French massal selection and never grafted, on colluvial granite soils with layers of clay.
wine.making: Every grape is destemmed by hand at the estate's gravity winery. Most of the wine ferments in French oak vats of 75 hectolitres, punched down by hand over four to five weeks on the skins, and goes through malolactic in new barrels. It then ages about two years in French barriques, most of them new, and is bottled without filtration.
wine.glass: Blackberry, blueberry and cassis with clove, black pepper and dried fig, then graphite, cedar, cocoa, leather and tobacco; full and velvety, with fine, polished tannin and a long, smoky finish.
wine.ageing: Made for a long life, by the house's sheets: decant a young bottle or give it several years in the cellar, after which it keeps developing for many more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, 17 by the house's sheets; decant a young bottle for at least an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Clos Apalta is Lapostolle's flagship: a Carmenère led blend from old, ungrafted vines on the Apalta hill, destemmed by hand and aged about two years in new French oak. Velvety, with cassis, black pepper and tobacco, it wants a decanter or a few years in the cellar.
records.story: The family behind Lapostolle made its name in liqueur: an ancestor, Louis-Alexandre Marnier Lapostolle (1857 to 1930), created Grand Marnier, cognac with bitter orange, in 1880. More than a century later his descendants looked to Chile, and in 1994 a couple of the family founded Lapostolle in the Colchagua Valley, with an old vineyard on the Apalta hill at its heart. Its vines had been planted early in the twentieth century from a French massal selection and never grafted. The first Clos Apalta followed with the 1997 vintage, a blend of Merlot, Carmenère and Cabernet Sauvignon. Carmenère, which Chile had long grown as Merlot until the two were told apart in 1994, came to lead the blend. A winery on the slope moves the wine by gravity, and every grape is destemmed by hand before it ferments in large oak vats. In 2008 Wine Spectator named the 2005 vintage its Wine of the Year, the first Chilean wine to be so named, and Clos Apalta became known far beyond Chile. The estate's vineyards are farmed organically and biodynamically. For a sommelier, Clos Apalta is the reference for Carmenère made to age, and the wine most often set beside Almaviva when Chile's flagships are listed.

wine.name: Casa Silva Microterroir de Los Lingues Carmenère
wine.grapes: Carmenère alone, from vines chosen one by one across the blocks of the vineyard.
wine.sites: The Los Lingues vineyard on the north eastern edge of the Colchagua Valley, in the Andean foothills near San Fernando: clay loam of alluvial and colluvial origin, low in organic matter and fertility, from fine sand to angular granite stones.
wine.making: On the house's sheet for 2021, the berries were sorted a second time and soaked cold for ten days, then fermented in French oak, in barrels of 500 litres and foudres of 1,000 litres, with a long maceration after. Malolactic followed in barrel, and the wine aged fifteen months in French oak.
wine.glass: Ripe red plum and blackberry with a hint of coffee and a soft touch of black pepper; deep ruby with a violet rim, supple, with good structure and soft tannin.
wine.ageing: Drinks well a few years after the vintage and, by the house's account, keeps for fifteen to twenty years.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Casa Silva's Microterroir de Los Lingues is Carmenère alone, from vines chosen block by block in the Andean foothills after a soil study the house began in 2005 with the University of Talca. Ripe and supple, with plum, coffee and black pepper, it shows the grape fully ripe.
records.story: The Silva family's vines in Colchagua go back to a French ancestor trained in Bordeaux, who reached Chile in the late nineteenth century and, by the family's account, bought the Angostura estate near San Fernando early in the twentieth. For decades his descendants grew grapes and sold their fruit and wine in bulk to larger houses. In the late 1970s the family began restoring the old vineyards and cellar, and in April 1997, on the proposal of the eldest son of the fifth generation, the family founded Viña Casa Silva to bottle the estate's wine under its own name. The house's vineyard at Los Lingues lies on the north eastern edge of the valley at the foot of the Andes, and in 2005 the house began a study of its soils and vines with the University of Talca, which the house describes as the first microterroir study in Chile. Plot by plot, the work showed which ground gave which fruit and guided the replanting, and the Microterroir Carmenère gathers the vines it picked out in each block. Los Lingues became an area of Chile's origin decree in 2018. For a sommelier the wine shows Carmenère from a cooler foothill site, picked ripe without the green edge, from a family that measured its ground before it named it.

wine.name: Viu 1
wine.grapes: Malbec, the great majority, with a little Cabernet Sauvignon and in some years a touch of Petit Verdot.
wine.sites: Block 4 of the house's San Carlos vineyard near Cunaco, an old planting of Malbec on alluvial, sandy clay soil with good drainage; the house dates the vines to more than a century ago.
wine.making: After a cold soak of about six days, the must ferments in small stainless steel tanks with short pump overs, about three weeks on the skins in all. The wine then ages about fifteen months in French oak, in recent editions partly in large untoasted foudres and partly in barriques.
wine.glass: Violet and fresh plum with blueberry and blackberry and a hint of graphite; balanced and concentrated, with fine, velvety tannin and a clear, persistent finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable on release after its time in oak, it keeps and develops for ten to twelve years, by the house's sheet for the 2020 edition.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant before serving, as the house advises; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Viu 1 is Viu Manent's Malbec from Block 4 of its San Carlos vineyard near Cunaco, old vines on sandy clay, aged about fifteen months in French oak. Violet and plum scented, with fine tannin, it comes from the house that, by its account, first bottled Malbec in Chile.
records.story: In 1935 a Catalan immigrant and his two sons founded Bodegas Viu in Santiago, bottling wine for Chilean tables under the Vinos Viu brand. The family wanted vineyards of its own, and in 1966 one of the sons bought the Hacienda San Carlos de Cunaco in the Colchagua Valley, an estate whose old vines, the house says, came from France before phylloxera. Among them were plots of Malbec. In 1993, by the house's account and by Wikipedia's, Viu Manent became the first Chilean winery to bottle, label and sell a wine of Malbec alone under the grape's name. The house then set its old Malbec block, Block 4 of the San Carlos vineyard, apart, and Viu 1 was first made from the 1999 vintage, as a tribute to the son who had bought the estate. Each vintage since is counted as an edition, the 2021 being the twentieth, and the bottles are numbered. A little Cabernet Sauvignon joins the Malbec, and recent editions age partly in large, untoasted foudres. For a sommelier, Viu 1 is the answer to a guest who thinks of Malbec as Argentina's alone: an old Colchagua block of Malbec, bottled under the grape's name.

wine.name: Neyen Espíritu de Apalta
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon and Carmenère, in near equal parts in the vintages read; early vintages leaned towards Carmenère and some carried a little Petit Verdot.
wine.sites: Old ungrafted vines on the Apalta estate, Cabernet Sauvignon planted in 1890 and Carmenère in 1936 by the house's account, on granite soils washed down from the hills and clay and silt laid by the river.
wine.making: Picked by hand early in the morning and sorted twice, the grapes ferment with native yeasts in tanks of 5,000 litres over three to four weeks. On the sheets read, each wine then spent about fourteen months in French barriques before blending and some six months more in a large foudre; later vintages also use concrete eggs.
wine.glass: Raspberry and blackcurrant with cedar, vanilla, leather and a subtle pepper; fresh and composed rather than heavy, with smooth tannin and a long, persistent finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable a few years after the vintage; most critics' windows close within about a decade, though the importer suggests ten years and more for a strong year.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The spirit of Apalta: the meaning of Neyen, the name the house says locals gave the hill's energy.

records.table: Neyen Espíritu de Apalta joins Cabernet Sauvignon and Carmenère in near equal parts from ungrafted Apalta vines planted in 1890 and 1936. Raspberry and blackcurrant with cedar and a subtle pepper, it is fresh rather than heavy and opens well after an hour in a decanter.
records.story: Vines came early to this corner of Apalta. By the house's account the estate's Cabernet Sauvignon was planted in 1890, and the walls of its old winery went up the same year, the oldest in the valley as the house tells it. Carmenère followed in 1936, and the vines were never grafted. Later in the twentieth century a family bought the property and, for decades, sold most of its fruit to others. In the early 2000s that family built a new winery on the estate and began to bottle a small share of the old vines' fruit under its own name: Neyen, which the house glosses as the spirit of Apalta, the energy locals feel on the hill. The blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Carmenère from the old vines has been Neyen's flagship ever since, its shares moving from vintage to vintage. In 2016 the Spanish sherry house González Byass bought a majority of Veramonte, the Chilean company that had taken in Neyen, and with it the Apalta estate. For a sommelier, Neyen shows what old ungrafted vines can give: Cabernet Sauvignon of 1890 and Carmenère of 1936 from one hill, poured together in one glass.
